arXiv|arxiv:2611.01799.title: Learning AI Agents, Market Makers, and Stress in Automated Markets
arXiv|arxiv:2611.01799.abstract: Automated markets increasingly route order flow from learning trading agents through automated market makers (AMMs). We model trader archetypes as AI agents defined by their reward functions and analyze the feedback they create on a constant-product AMM. Herd-dominated and arbitrage-dominated markets of equal size have identical return distributions and turnover, so no rule based on volatility, value-at-risk, stress frequency, or volume can tell them apart; yet their stress episodes differ in length by a factor unbounded in the feedback-to-noise ratio $β/s$. Serial statistics identify the feedback sign from $Θ((s/β)^2\log(1/δ))$ observations, and this rate is tight. When agents trade together, profit-seeking agents ride herds rather than lean against them, leading to all-or-nothing participation. Spread-earning market makers restore stability but make liquidity fragile, with discontinuous collapse and hysteresis; maker--taker pricing, not a uniform fee, is the effective instrument.

arXiv|arxiv:2602.16444.title: RoboGene: Diversity-Driven Agentic Task Generation Framework for VLA Pre-training
arXiv|arxiv:2602.16444.abstract: The pursuit of general-purpose robotic manipulation is hindered by the scarcity of diverse, real-world interaction data. Unlike large-scale web vision-language data, robotic data collection incurs prohibitive physical costs. The key challenge is thus not merely to collect more robot data, but to obtain informative training data that broadens behavioral coverage across objects, scenes, and skills. Yet automatically curating task proposals to maximize the utility of collected data remains under-explored. We introduce RoboGene, an agentic framework for generating diverse, informative manipulation tasks across single-arm, dual-arm, and mobile robots. RoboGene combines (1) diversity-driven sampling for broad task coverage, (2) agentic self-reflection for task-quality assessment, and (3) human-verified feedback memory for execution-grounded validation and continual refinement. Through quantitative analysis and large-scale real-world experiments, we collect 18k trajectories and introduce metrics for task feasibility and diversity. RoboGene significantly outperforms frontier foundation models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Pro. VLA models trained on RoboGene-generated data achieve higher success rates and stronger generalization, highlighting the value of high-quality task generation. Project page: https://robogene-boost-vla.github.io/. Datasets: Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/X-Humanoid/RoboGene) and ModelScope (https://modelscope.cn/datasets/X-Humanoid/RoboGene_tasks).

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: Leveraging robust optimization for llm alignment under distribution shifts
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Preference alignment methods are increasingly critical for steering large language models (LLMs) to generate outputs consistent with human values. While recent approaches often rely on synthetic data generated by LLMs for scalability and cost-efficiency reasons, this reliance can introduce distributional shifts that undermine the nuanced representation of human preferences needed for desirable outputs. In this paper, we propose a novel distribution-aware optimization framework that improves preference alignment despite such shifts. Our approach first leverages well-learned classifiers to assign a calibration value to each training sample, quantifying its alignment with the target human-preferred distribution. These values are then incorporated into a robust optimization objective that minimizes the worst-case loss over regions of the data space most relevant to human preferences. By explicitly focusing optimization on the target distribution, our approach mitigates the impact of distributional mismatch and improves the generation of responses that better reflect intended values.

ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.title: Towards Detecting AI-Assisted Responses in Online Surveys
ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.abstract: The use of LLMs to complete online surveys impacts the validity of survey-based research, but detecting such usage remains under-explored. We introduce an initial benchmark dataset, namely ASURRE, for AI-assisted survey participation to capture usage strategies ranging from full generation and revision to persona-grounded agentic completion. Controlled by these strategies, LLM-assisted survey responses are generated using multiple LLMs on three real-world surveys in different disciplines, paired with genuine human responses. Our evaluation of existing machine-generated text (MGT) detectors shows that naive AI usage is readily detectable, whereas persona-grounded agents that mimic entire respondents push detector performance toward chance. We further show that agentic completion cannot fully replicate respondent-level behaviour and leaves distinctive behavioural traces. While individual cues can be circumvented by targeted prompting, a simple few-shot, training-free aggregator over these cues improves mean AUROC by +0.14 over the best existing detector across agentic settings. Our project is available on GitHub.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.02609.title: Whitened Advantage Summation Policy Optimization: Correlation-Aware Aggregation for Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning
arXiv|arxiv:2611.02609.abstract: Reinforcement learning for language models often combines several rewards by normalizing each one and adding them with fixed weights. When the rewards are correlated, the variation they share is counted once for every reward that carries it. In terms of the ZCA-decorrelated components of the reward signal, the weighted sum applies weights $Σ^{1/2} w$ rather than the chosen weights $w$, where $Σ$ is the reward correlation matrix. We study WAS-PO, which whitens the normalized advantages with $Σ^{-1/2}$ before adding them, so that the chosen weights apply to those components. We derive the scalarized objective whose gradient it follows when normalization statistics are held fixed, show that its weights on the raw rewards can be negative, give an exact two-reward condition under which the lighter-weighted reward is reversed, and give a loose bound on the error from estimating $Σ$ during training. On tool calling with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, WAS-PO reached a higher mean training reward than GDPO in all seven seeds with three rewards (3.8% higher) and all three seeds with four (3.9% higher). WAS-PO also replaces GDPO's per-prompt normalization with batch-level normalization, and we did not separate the two changes with three or four rewards. The training-reward gains did not carry over to held-out accuracy, which was slightly lower than GDPO's with three rewards (not significant) and 0.03 lower in absolute terms with four (two seeds evaluated). With two rewards, WAS-PO trailed GDPO in training reward, and a three-seed control weakly suggests that the gap comes from batch-level normalization rather than whitening. In a math setting where the two rewards were nearly identical by construction, WAS-PO drove down the lighter-weighted reward, as the sign condition predicts.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.22942.title: An Evolutionary Agentic Approach for Open-ended Image Quality Perception
arXiv|arxiv:2609.22942.abstract: Generative models are rapidly expanding image quality assessment (IQA) beyond traditional fidelity factors to emerging dimensions such as physical plausibility and text-rendering correctness. However, existing IQA models rely on fixed definitions and heavy supervision, making them difficult to extend to open-ended perceptual dimensions. We identify holistic bias as an important limitation: when scoring an unseen dimension, models reuse generic quality priors, leading to scoring errors and rank inversion. To address this, we propose PACE (Perceptual Agentic Collaborative Evolution), a training-free multi-agent framework that formulates open-ended IQA as explicit protocol construction. Given a target dimension, PACE uses collaborative agents to construct an evaluation protocol composed of verifiable Visual Question Answering (VQA) probes, grounding evaluation in concrete visual evidence rather than holistic impressions. The resulting protocol is calibrated using only four human-annotated images per dimension, while a dual-track scoring mechanism aligns model perception with human scoring scales. Across traditional IQA, structural fidelity, context-aware aesthetics, and newly defined open-ended dimensions, PACE consistently improves its MLLM backbone, achieving competitive performance across diverse IQA settings, and reduces the Holistic Override Rate (HOR) from 44.4\% to 8.6\%.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: When Do Multi-Agent Systems Help? An Information Bottleneck Perspective
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: LLM powered multi-agent systems (MAS) have emerged as a promising paradigm for complex tasks. However, their advantages over single-agent systems (SAS) remain unclear, with performance varying inconsistently across settings. Here, we provide an information bottleneck perspective on elucidating the differences between MAS and SAS. Specifically, our key observation is that a SAS accumulates its full reasoning trace in one shared context, while a MAS uses isolated local contexts connected by bounded relay messages. We show that, under infinite relay bandwidth, any SAS can be emulated by a MAS that transmits the full upstream context. Thus, the nontrivial advantage of MAS arises under bounded relays, where compression introduces a fundamental trade-off: reducing redundant context can improve efficiency, but may also incur loss of task-relevant information. We formalize this trade-off as an information bottleneck controlled by an effective parameter $\beta$, which captures how the balance shifts with model capability, and shows that MAS gains arise when context reduction outweighs relay information loss. We conduct 18 controlled experiments across five benchmarks and three model scales to validate our theoretical studies. We observe that MAS consistently helps when relays are near-sufficient, especially for weaker models. In contrast, MAS gains shrink or reverse when relays incur information loss, especially for stronger models that can already extract useful information from redundant context and thus gain little from compression. Our study shows that multi-agent design is fundamentally an information-bottleneck optimization problem. This perspective explains when bounded inter-agent communication helps or hurts.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.19051.title: Smart Alone, Blind Together: Why Accuracy Fails to CertifyTheory of Mind in Multi-Agent Teams
arXiv|arxiv:2610.19051.abstract: Coordinators that act on what they infer about teammates are usually certified by the accuracy of those inferences. We argue that accuracy is the wrong certificate, for two reasons. First, the accuracy needed to act depends on what a wrong action costs, so the bar belongs to the deployment, not the module. Second, a module's errors are rarely independent, and dependence has a sign: positively associated errors help where their damage overlaps and hurt where it compounds, so an accuracy threshold fails in a predictable direction, and once wrong beliefs interact and can do harm, no rule based on accuracy is right for every module. We test these predictions in task assignment, Level-Based Foraging and Hanabi, with injected errors, trained and Bayesian modules and five language models, and in human judgments. Accuracy fails in both directions, approving harmful language-model deployments in Hanabi, where shared errors compound, and rejecting beneficial ones in task assignment, where costly errors are rare. In our tasks it also buys far less redundancy than independence predicts: from GPT-5.4-mini to Claude Opus 5.5, error on teammates the models have evidence about falls from 32% to 11%, but the chance that all three observers misread one falls only from 16% to 9% (independence: 3.4% to 0.15%). We propose certifying the deployment, with a Blind-Spot Gate that prices error costs, pairwise interactions and measured dependence without deploying the module. On held-out data from the cells it was developed on, it makes no significant false approval in 20 splits (accuracy: 3.2 per split), and in preregistered tests on modules it was not developed on, it recovers what accuracy rejects (seven classifiers: regret 0.004 against 0.479) and catches what accuracy approves (a Bayesian module: significant false approvals in 17 of 20 splits for accuracy, 1 for the gate).

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: HyperAgents
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Self-improving AI systems aim to reduce reliance on human engineering by learning to improve their own learning and problem-solving processes. Existing approaches to self-improvement rely on fixed, handcrafted meta-level mechanisms, fundamentally limiting how fast such systems can improve. The Darwin G\"odel Machine (DGM) achieves open-ended self-improvement in coding, but this relies on domain-specific alignment between task performance and self-modification skill. However, this alignment does not generally hold beyond coding domains. We introduce \textbf{hyperagents}, self-referential agents that integrate a task agent (which solves the target task) and a meta agent (which modifies itself and the task agent) into a single editable program. Crucially, the meta-level modification procedure is itself editable, enabling metacognitive self-modification, improving not only the task-solving behavior, but also the mechanism that generates future improvements. We instantiate this framework by extending DGM to create DGM-Hyperagents (DGM-H), eliminating the need for domain-specific alignment to potentially support self-accelerating progress on any computable task. Across diverse domains, the DGM-H improves performance over time and outperforms baselines without self-improvement or open-ended exploration, as well as prior self-improving systems. Furthermore, the DGM-H improves the process by which it generates new agents (e.g., persistent memory, performance tracking), and these meta-level improvements transfer across domains and accumulate across runs. All experiments were conducted with safety precautions (e.g., sandboxing, human oversight). We discuss what safety entails in this setting and the broader implications of self-improving systems. DGM-Hyperagents offer a glimpse of open-ended AI systems that do not merely search for better solutions, but continually improve their search for how to improve.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.27664.title: Evolutionary Stability Does Not Guarantee Learning Accessibility: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Perspective on Cooperation Emergence
arXiv|arxiv:2609.27664.abstract: Cooperation emergence is a central problem in multi-agent systems because decentralized agents must coordinate while adapting to the changing behavior of others. Evolutionary game theory identifies strategically stable outcomes, but stability under a population adjustment dynamic need not imply that finite-sample learning agents can reach the same outcome through local reward feedback. We study this distinction in a transparent three-agent governance-motivated game involving a government, a platform firm, and users. We derive replicator dynamics for the fixed stage-game incentives, evaluate the cooperative evolutionary basin on a symmetric initial-condition grid, and compare it with learning-basin estimates for three decentralized value-based learners. The learning analysis uses independent Q-learning with $\varepsilon$-greedy action selection, scaled Boltzmann exploration, and SA--EA BQL under the same payoff environment and outcome criterion. The evolutionary basin has volume $V_E=1.00$ on the sampled grid. The empirical learning basin is $0.88$ for $\varepsilon$-IQL and $0.00$ for both scaled Boltzmann and SA--EA BQL. Diagnostic traces show that broader action diversity and nonzero value separation can coexist with failure to sustain the cooperative joint action in this fixed configuration. These results indicate that evolutionary stability and learning accessibility are distinct properties of a coupled game--learning system. The shared-bike setting is a motivating application; the broader contribution is a framework for comparing population-level stability with the finite-sample accessibility of cooperation under specified multi-agent learning dynamics.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.12314.title: A Modular Perspective for Modeling MARL Systems
arXiv|arxiv:2611.12314.abstract: The growing complexity of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has fragmented the literature, obscuring underlying architectural choices behind diverse implementations. This fragmentation makes it difficult to evaluate critical modeling dimensions in isolation, identify how components affect the resulting system dynamics, and compare, reuse, or combine contributions across the literature. This paper proposes a modular perspective for modeling, analyzing, and implementing MARL systems. We decompose them into eight functional modules: agents, environments, learning, reward modeling, training and execution modes, communication, modeling of other agents, and evaluation criteria. For each module, we clarify its role and review representative approaches. We instantiate this decomposition in MARLKIT, a framework whose modules are explicit and interchangeable. MARLKIT demonstrates how the proposed perspective supports transparent experimental assumptions and the controlled variation and combination of MARL mechanisms. Experiments illustrate its ability to prototype, compare, reuse and combine modules while making differences between configurations explicit. Overall, the paper provides a structured perspective on MARL modeling and implementation, offering a common language for making modeling choices explicit, supporting clearer descriptions of MARL approaches, and supporting more controlled experimentation through the systematic isolation and combination of MARL mechanisms.

ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.abstract: Agentic RAG, which decomposes a complex question into dependency-aware sub-questions, has become the dominant paradigm for multi-hop QA. arXiv|arxiv:2611.03301.title: An Axiomatic Framework for Reinforcement Learning in Open Multi-Agent Systems
arXiv|arxiv:2611.03301.abstract: Open multi-agent systems, where only a subset of agents are controllable, are central to real-world domains such as smart grids, yet lack a principled foundation for reinforcement learning algorithm design. We study this setting through n-agent ad hoc teamwork (NAHT), a recent framework for learning in open multi-agent environments. We propose an axiomatic framework that derives value function learning from the Shapley axioms (Efficiency, Symmetry and Linearity), treating them as structural constraints rather than heuristic design choices. This formulation builds on a novel NAHT decomposition, which characterises the fundamental difference between open and fully controllable multi-agent systems, and establishes a cooperative game-theoretic foundation for learning. We further show that enforcing these axioms on learning individual value functions recovers the Shapley value for Dec-POMDPs, providing a principled bridge between reinforcement learning and classical cooperative game theory. Building on this framework, we introduce Shapley Machines and Banzhaf Machines, two generic algorithmic templates that can be instantiated with standard reinforcement learning methods. When applied to strong base algorithms such as IPPO and POAM, our methods consistently improve learning efficiency and generalisation to unseen agent types and conventions across NAHT benchmark tasks. The code of experiments is published on https://github.com/hsvgbkhgbv/axiomatic-rl-naht.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.00541.title: Random Recursive Models
arXiv|arxiv:2610.00541.abstract: Recursive models create computational depth through parameter reuse, offering a parameter-efficient alternative to increasing model size. However, most recursive models repeatedly apply one learned transformation or a prescribed sequence of transformations, restricting computation to a fixed layer order. We introduce the Random Recursive Model (RRM), which maintains a pool of $L$ learned layers and performs $T$ recursive steps by sampling one layer independently with replacement for each example and step. This enables flexible layer reuse while retaining the parameter efficiency of recurrence. We evaluate RRM on challenging reasoning tasks, where it matches or exceeds the baselines, often with 50-75 % fewer parameters. RRM can vary its depth at inference, including beyond that seen during training, without retraining or adding parameters, improving tasks that benefit from deeper iterative computation. RRM also supports Monte Carlo inference and probabilistic test-time scaling, both of which improve performance without retraining. These insights may open new directions in neural network architecture design.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: Multi-Stream LLMs: Unblocking Language Models with Parallel Streams of Thoughts, Inputs and Outputs
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: The continued improvements in language model capability have unlocked their widespread use as drivers of autonomous agents, for example in coding or computer use applications. However, the core of these systems has not changed much since early instruction-tuned models like ChatGPT. Even advanced AI agents function on message exchange formats, successively exchanging messages with users, systems, with itself (i.e. chain-of-thought) and tools in a single stream of computation. This bottleneck to a **single stream** as in chat models leads to a number of limitations: the agent cannot act (generate output) while reading, and in reverse, cannot react to new information while writing. Similarly, the agent cannot act while thinking and cannot think while reading or acting on information. In this work, we show that models can be unblocked by switching from instruction-tuning for sequential message formats to instruction-tuning for **multiple, parallel streams of computation**, splitting each **role** into a separate stream. Every forward pass of the language model then simultaneously reads from multiple input streams and generates tokens in multiple output streams, all of which causally depend on earlier timesteps. We argue that this data-driven change remedies a number of usability limitations as outlined above, improves model efficiency through parallelization, improves model security through better separation of concerns and improves model monitorability.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.04434.title: Sketchpad: certified exact arithmetic with a small vision-language model
arXiv|arxiv:2611.04434.abstract: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated on samples and carries no guarantee for an unseen input; tool use is exact but moves the computation outside the network. We show that exactness at all input lengths becomes a finite, checkable property of a network when each of its steps reads only a bounded view of an external working memory. In Sketchpad, Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter executes arithmetic procedures on a rendered sheet. Each forward pass reads a three-cell view and emits one step: a digit, a carry or borrow, and the next operation. A fixed runtime moves the view and writes no digit of a result. We prove in Lean that the model is then exact on all inputs of any length if and only if it is exact on the finite set of views the runtime presents, that no finite test suffices when steps also read earlier steps, and that the guarantee tolerates bounded numerical perturbation and extends to compositions of procedures. All 2,446 views pass on the deployment device, a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser. The certified model performs signed addition and subtraction, long multiplication and division, square roots and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length. It solved 200 of 200 pre-registered problems in the browser, and 220 of 220 sums of up to 1,000 digits and products of up to 20 digits, of which GPT-6.1 Sol, the strongest of ten other models, solved 217. A symbolic runtime built on these procedures solves, expands and factors polynomials with every number computed by the model, and a multiplicative gate on the adapter recovers the base model exactly when the sheet is not in use.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.06695.title: MedPrune: Topology-Efficient Multimodal Multi-Agent Communication Evolution for Medical VQA Tasks
arXiv|arxiv:2610.06695.abstract: While medical multimodal large language models (Med-MLLMs) advance medical visual question answering (VQA), existing clinical workflow-inspired multi-agent frameworks suffer from interaction patterns and excessive computational overhead caused by redundant communication topologies. In this paper, we propose MedPrune, an efficient medical multimodal multi-agent collaboration framework that dynamically prunes both nodes and edges from the communication topology to enhance reasoning ability and token efficiency. Specifically, we first formulate the diagnostic process as a heterogeneous communication graph, where nodes represent specialist agents from various departments and edges capture intra- and inter-departmental interactions. Building on this graph, we introduce two sparsification mechanisms to enable adaptive collaborative evolution: (1) Heterogeneous Node Sparsification, which eliminates task-irrelevant specialist agents irrelevant to the current multimodal question via reinforcement learning-driven topological optimization, and (2) Heterogeneous Edge Sparsification, which selectively retains only the most diagnostically salient intra- and inter-departmental connections by jointly optimizing task performance and topological complexity. Extensive medical VQA experiments under full-set and few-shot training settings prove MedPrune surpasses multi-agent baselines and boosts token efficiency with strong adversarial robustness.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.03966.abstract: Tool-use evaluations typically measure calls through a serving stack, which can report zero calls even when model outputs contain call-shaped payloads. We study interface-induced trajectory censoring: a mismatch between model emissions and the interface that converts them into actions. On selected BFCL v4 subsets, changing only the serving adapter while holding model weights and other evaluation settings fixed moves scores under the official scorer from 0.00 to 0.96 on simple_python and from 0.00 to 0.19 on multi_turn_base. A template-parser factorial experiment shows strong complementarity: neither component replacement alone restores parsing from the baseline, whereas their joint replacement recovers 196/200 first-request parses. Across five Qwen2.5-Coder checkpoints, classifier-positive emissions increase with model size while the mismatched interface reports no calls; a separate matched-interface Qwen3 ladder exhibits few silent emissions through 8B. Experiments on 115 tau-bench retail tasks extend the mechanism to a stateful, non-code environment. In a preregistered, single-seed, 150-step 7B LoRA experiment, changing only the parser registered in verl increases tool executions from 10 to 16,844. However, neither a shared programmatic-feedback evaluation nor a post-hoc common native function-calling evaluation detects a held-out success gain from repair; rescue counts do not increase. Interface repair thus restores tool-mediated experience without a detected performance gain in this setting. These findings show that tool-use measurements depend on the model-interface configuration and motivate layer-wise observability and conformance checks before attributing evaluation or training outcomes to the model alone.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.18843.title: LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models
arXiv|arxiv:2610.18843.abstract: Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment environments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and remounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot's hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. The benchmark spans eleven perturbation axes, including camera mounting and optics, camera-to-arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, proprioceptive noise, base pose, table height, and gripper pads. Each axis has five severity levels, yielding 210 conditions across the four LIBERO suites. We evaluate nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and substantiate each finding with rigorous statistical tests. Pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at the middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Performance degradation varies substantially across perturbation axes and action interfaces, and training on visual perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged. We release the benchmark together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation parameters for each episode.

arXiv|arxiv:2508.10447.abstract: Estimating input-dependent probability surfaces from binary, binomial, categorical, or multinomial response data is a common task in statistics and machine learning. PMLR|https://proceedings.mlr.press/v306/.abstract: Test-Time Scaling (TTS) improves LLM reasoning by exploring multiple candidate responses and then operating over this set to find the best output. A tacit premise behind TTS is that sufficiently diverse candidate pools enhance reliability. In this work, we show that this assumption in TTS introduces a previously unrecognized failure mode. When candidate diversity is curtailed, even by a modest amount, TTS becomes much more likely to produce unsafe outputs. We present a reference-guided diversity reduction protocol (RefDiv) that serves as a diagnostic attack to stress test TTS pipelines. Through extensive experiments across open-source models (e.g. Qwen3, Mistral, Llama3.1, Gemma3) and two widely used TTS strategies (Monte Carlo Tree Search and Best-of-N), constraining diversity consistently signifies the rate at which TTS produces unsafe results. This observed phenomenon also transfers across TTS strategies and to closed-source models (e.g. OpenAI o3-mini and Gemini-2.5-Pro), thus indicating that this is a general and extant property of TTS rather than a model-specific artifact. Additionally, we find that numerous widely used safety guardrail classifiers (e.g. Llama-Guard), are unable to flag the adversarial input prompts generated by RefDiv, demonstrating that existing defenses offer limited protection against this diversity-driven failure mode.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.40370.title: The Athlete as a Scientist of One: Agentic Bayesian Experimental Design for Individualized Physiology from Consumer Wearables
arXiv|arxiv:2610.40370.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for personal health read wearable data and recommend, but do not learn about the individual in a way that can be audited or falsified. We present EpiCoach, an agentic system that treats one athlete, a cross-country mountain biker, as the subject of accountable N-of-1 science. Claims about the athlete live in an evidence-gated hypothesis registry: each must issue a probabilistic prediction about a future session before it occurs, and its belief moves only through computed evidence from a logged statistical fit. Predictions come from a mechanistic digital twin inferred from heart rate, GPS and barometric altitude: a lagged heart-rate response model, a fitness-fatigue model with learned time constants, and a latent technical-descending skill state, measured on discovered trail segments. The agent prescribes the next training week as a constrained experiment maximizing information gain subject to load and safety constraints, around two instrument rides. We evaluate the system two ways over eighteen months of data. A rolling-origin replay benchmark shows the twin beats standard forecasters on heart rate but not segment time, and the agentic loop matches a static model. A live prospective phase runs the weekly cycle: in its first three weeks the ledger sealed 20 predictions, scored 14, the descent forecast calibrated after one correction, the climb forecast pessimistic as the athlete improved, and the safety officer vetoed the agent twice. Every correction is preserved in the registry, a template for auditable, falsifiable personalization in digital health. We release the registry, benchmark and protocol.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: PACE: Two-Timescale Self-Evolution for Small Language Model Agents
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Deploying language-model agents in production often requires substantial compute and human effort to tune prompts, parsers, validators, and other components of the agent pipeline. Self-evolution offers a promising alternative, but most existing frameworks assume access to frontier models that can reliably diagnose failures, propose revisions, and judge their own updates. We study whether frozen small language models (SLMs) can serve as effective self-evolving agents under resource constraints. We propose PACE (Prompt And Control Logic Evolution), a two-timescale framework that coordinates low-risk prompt refinement with higher-risk control-logic updates. PACE evolves prompts under fixed control logic until prompt-level gains saturate, then considers constrained control-logic updates that are accepted through held-out validation. Across three frozen SLM backbones ranging from 4B to 14B parameters and four controlled benchmarks, PACE achieves the best performance on all 12 backbone--benchmark combinations, improving over vanilla SLM agents by up to $+9.2\%$ relative improvement and over the stronger single-mode evolution baseline by up to $+5.4\%$ relative improvement. A $\tau$-bench case study further shows that PACE improves multi-turn tool-use success over vanilla and prompt-only evolution. These results suggest that reliable SLM agent self-evolution is possible without updating model weights or relying on frontier-model teachers, and that the key benefit is not any single final solver pattern but autonomous, validated discovery of task-appropriate inference strategies.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.21016.title: CausalEvo: Causal Skill Self-Evolution for Health LLM Agents
arXiv|arxiv:2610.21016.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for health can accumulate reusable textual skills from task feedback, such as calculation criteria, measurement time points, and formula units. Deciding which skills to retain is consequential: useful rules improve later answers, while faulty generalizations propagate errors. We propose CausalEvo, a method for causal skill self-evolution that estimates the relative effects of deliberately changed skill sets while holding the model weights, feedback cases, and rule count fixed. At each evolution step, a frozen LLM proposes candidate rules, which are pooled with the incumbent skills so that the current skill set remains a feasible choice. Paired skill replacements against shared background rules are scored on the same feedback cases; least squares converts the score differences into relative skill values, and the top-ranked rules are retained, favoring incumbents on ties. A decision-loss bound separates candidate support, approximation, and estimation errors. On six MedCalc-Bench-Verified tasks with 120 held-out cases, CausalEvo achieves 60.00% accuracy, compared with 55.83% for SkillOpt and 51.67% without skills. Across the recorded training configurations, which use different optimization budgets, it consumes 55.6% fewer training tokens than SkillOpt. Gains concentrate in particular calculations alongside regressions on others, and paired accuracy intervals include zero. CausalEvo turns task feedback into controlled decisions about skill retention and replacement. Project repository: https://github.com/txbrook/CausalEvo

CVF|https://openaccess.thecvf.com/conten.abstract: Few-shot Class-Incremental Learning (FSCIL) challenges models to adapt to new classes with limited samples, presenting greater difficulties than traditional classincremental learning. arXiv|arxiv:2610.25693.title: ToolOPD: Credit-Aware On-Policy Distillation for Tool-Use Agents
arXiv|arxiv:2610.25693.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) enhances the capabilities of small language agents by providing dense, token-level supervision from a teacher model on student-generated trajectories. However, standard OPD implicitly assumes that credit is uniformly distributed across long-horizon trajectories, assigning the same strength of teacher supervision to different actions. Through credit-distribution analysis and outcome-reversal counterfactual experiments, we find that trajectory credit is concentrated on a small number of critical actions. Moreover, even when the trajectory is held fixed, reversing only the final outcome substantially changes the credit assigned to multiple interaction turns. These findings show that the uniform-credit assumption fails to identify critical decisions and ultimately degrades the model's reasoning accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose ToolOPD, an outcome-aware on-policy distillation framework designed for long-horizon tool use. ToolOPD first summarizes each completed trajectory and its outcome into a reusable hindsight skill. It then measures how this skill changes the teacher's probability of each student action token and converts the change into outcome-aware credit. The resulting credit preserves supervision that supports successful decisions or discourages failed ones, while suppressing irrelevant and conflicting signals. ToolOPD uses these credits to reweight the action-level distillation loss and jointly optimizes it with reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across multiple long-horizon tool interaction benchmarks demonstrate that ToolOPD significantly outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines.

arXiv|arxiv:2607.12075.title: Calibrated selective prediction using deep ensembles for thyroid nodule ultrasound classification under dataset shift
arXiv|arxiv:2607.12075.abstract: Background: Deep learning can classify thyroid nodules on ultrasound, but discrimination alone does not establish clinical reliability. We developed a calibrated deep-ensemble framework with uncertainty-aware selective prediction and conservative image-based triage. Methods: Nested five-fold cross-validation with three-fold inner architecture selection chose ConvNeXt-Tiny with a squeeze-and-excitation block, used to build a deterministic five-member ensemble. Training, early-stopping, calibration, and threshold subsets were separated within each fold; outer-test data remained isolated. Mutual information (MI), predictive variance, and maximum-softmax-probability (MSP) uncertainty were compared by risk-coverage and triage analyses, and predictive values across assumed malignancy prevalences of 5%-70%. The frozen TN5000 ensemble was applied to TN3K without recalibration. Results: On TN5000, pooled out-of-fold AUC-ROC was 0.9377, average precision 0.9708, expected calibration error 0.0138, and Brier score 0.0827. Under the primary MI-guided policy, 8.86% of images received a No-FNA suggestion, 60.00% an FNA recommendation, and 31.14% radiologist review; of 3574 malignant images, 14 (0.39%) received No-FNA and 708 (19.81%) review. Predictive variance and MSP ranked errors better than MI (AURC, AUGRC); no measure optimized all triage outcomes. Across prevalences of 5%-70%, NPV ranged 99.95%-97.93% and PPV 29.28%-94.75%. On TN3K, AUC-ROC was 0.7870, average precision 0.7254, expected calibration error 0.1899, and radiologist-review rate 83.7%. Conclusion: The ensemble showed strong internal discrimination and calibration, but performance deteriorated substantially on TN3K, indicating limited transportability under dataset shift. Multicentre validation, site-specific recalibration, threshold validation, and prospective evaluation are needed before clinical use.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: PolyMind: Exploring Width Scaling for Reflective Reasoning in Language Agents
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Reflection-based language agents improve reasoning by using feedback to revise previous attempts across multiple trials. Most existing reflection frameworks scale this process by \emph{depth}, allocating additional test-time compute to longer serial reflection-retry chains. However, we observe that serial reflection often saturates after rapid early gains. Under controlled reflection budgets, increasing depth from $5$ to $10$ cycles brings only marginal improvement, yet isolated reflective workers still contain useful revision signals beyond the saturated chain. This raises a central question: can reflective reasoning scale by \emph{width} rather than only by depth? A direct answer is non-trivial, since naive parallel reflection often inspects similar aspects of the same failed attempt and produces long or noisy revision contexts after aggregation. We propose \ourmethod, a reflective width scaling framework that learns to allocate complementary reflective scopes, execute workers in isolated contexts, and compress parallel feedback into a structured PolyBrief. \ourmethod trains the planner, workers, and reducer with verifiable outcome feedback and a role-balanced objective that prevents wider rollouts from dominating optimization. Across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-hop question answering, \ourmethod consistently improves performance under matched reflection budgets, outperforming the strongest depth-reflection baseline by an average of $6.1\%$. Further analyses show that \ourmethod closes about $80\%$ of the oracle-naive width gap, reduces redundant worker outputs, and improves revision success with fewer tokens. These results suggest that reflection should be understood not only as a longer retry process, but also as a depth-width compute allocation problem.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.29331.title: From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context?
arXiv|arxiv:2610.29331.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied across the scientific discovery pipeline, from synthesizing literature to generating hypotheses to informing experimental design. A unifying principle behind these tasks is the need to continuously update beliefs as evidence accumulates, for which Bayesian inference provides a natural framework. However, existing work assumes that LLMs cannot carry out principled Bayesian belief updating in context, instead relying on simplifications and heuristics. To challenge this assumption, we present a principled evaluation of Bayesian reasoning capabilities in LLMs, analyzing both the model's internal consistency as well as its ability to recover an externally determined posterior. Specifically, we build an evaluation framework spanning qualitative epistemological examples to probe probabilistic coherence, quantitative benchmarks of Bayesian inference capabilities, and analyses of the impact of non-Bayesian updates on downstream task performance. Across different scenarios, we find that LLMs generally violate Bayes' rule when updating their beliefs in context. However, when equipped with modern reasoning abilities and code execution capabilities, their performance drastically improves, enabling even the close approximation of analytically intractable posteriors. Our evaluation shows that current LLMs with access to appropriate tools could already be used to make complex belief updates in scientific discovery, enabling rapid acceleration of the efficiency and scale of AI-powered scientific discovery.

A unifying principle behind these tasks is the need to continuously update beliefs as evidence accumulates, for which Bayesian inference provides a natural framework. However, existing work assumes that LLMs cannot carry out principled Bayesian belief updating in context, instead relying on simplifications and heuristics. To challenge this assumption, we present a principled evaluation of Bayesian reasoning capabilities in LLMs, analyzing both the model's internal consistency as well as its ability to recover an externally determined posterior. Specifically, we build an evaluation framework spanning qualitative epistemological examples to probe probabilistic coherence, quantitative benchmarks of Bayesian inference capabilities, and analyses of the impact of non-Bayesian updates on downstream task performance. Across different scenarios, we find that LLMs generally violate Bayes' rule when updating their beliefs in context. However, when equipped with modern reasoning abilities and code execution capabilities, their performance drastically improves, enabling even the close approximation of analytically intractable posteriors. Our evaluation shows that current LLMs with access to appropriate tools could already be used to make complex belief updates in scientific discovery, enabling rapid acceleration of the efficiency and scale of AI-powered scientific discovery.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.38418.title: PneuTac: Tactile Manipulation with Soft Pneumatic Robots via Unified MPM-Gaussian Splatting Simulation
arXiv|arxiv:2609.38418.abstract: Soft robots and tactile sensors have demonstrated great potential in delicate manipulation tasks. Soft pneumatic robots enable safe contact through compliance, and vision-based tactile sensors offer high-resolution touch perception. However, learning tactile manipulation with compliant robots has been challenging, bottlenecked by the lack of efficient simulation. Existing simulators typically model them in isolation, and exhibit large calibration gaps that are difficult to overcome efficiently. We present PneuTac, a unified framework for tactile-feedback manipulation with soft pneumatic robots. We leverage the material point method (MPM) for modelling the dynamics of the soft robot and the deformable tactile membrane, and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) for rendering. Real-to-sim modelling is done with a simple vision-based method, to then train action and perception networks for efficient simulation with surrogate models. We use the framework to drive a tactile-guided pipeline to collect demonstrations in simulation. Through experiments on a custom-designed pneumatic soft finger with a tactile sensing tip, together with additional cross-device evaluations, we show that PneuTac is capable of accurately modelling soft robots with tactile sensors, and that policies trained with simulation-augmented demonstrations outperform baselines trained on the same real data on three real-world contact-rich compliant manipulation tasks, making it a practical framework for tactile manipulation on compliant hardware.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Multi-Agent Pathfinding
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) focuses on determining conflict-free paths for multiple agents navigating through a shared space to reach specified goal locations. This problem becomes computationally challenging, particularly when handling large numbers of agents, as frequently encountered in practical applications like coordinating autonomous vehicles. Quantum Computing (QC) is a promising candidate in overcoming such limits. However, current quantum hardware is still in its infancy and thus limited in terms of computing power and error robustness. In this work, we present the first optimal hybrid quantum-classical MAPF algorithms which are based on branch-and-cut-and-prize. QC is integrated by iteratively solving QUBO problems, based on conflict graphs. Experiments on actual quantum hardware and results on benchmark data suggest that our approach dominates previous QUBO formulations and state-of-the-art MAPF solvers.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.15274.title: Embodiment-Aware Inference-Time Search for Human Reaction Selection in Humanoid Retargeting
arXiv|arxiv:2610.15274.abstract: Training humanoid robots to learn human behaviors requires expensive data collection, and human-robot interaction data can be even more difficult and costly to collect. Training a specialized reaction model for each humanoid embodiment can also be time-consuming and resource-intensive. Human-to-humanoid motion retargeting provides a more scalable alternative, allowing human-human reaction data to serve as a common motion representation for different humanoid embodiments. However, due to morphological and kinematic differences between humans and humanoid robots, a reaction preferred in human motion space may not be the most suitable one for execution on a particular robot embodiment. In this work, we propose an inference-time reaction search framework that leverages stochastic sampling from a generative reaction model and jointly considers reaction quality and humanoid embodiment feasibility. Given the observed interaction, our framework generates multiple plausible reaction candidates. Each candidate is retargeted to the target humanoid and evaluated using complementary interaction and embodiment-specific feasibility criteria, allowing candidate selection under the physical constraints of the target embodiment. Since the reaction generator remains frozen, the framework can adapt to different humanoid embodiments at inference time without retraining. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework maintains overall human reaction quality while improving the feasibility of retargeted humanoid reactions across different embodiments. The proposed pipeline improves humanoid retargeting feasibility by 1.61%. Moreover, human-space and G1 best-candidate selections disagree in 78.98% of samples, demonstrating substantial embodiment dependence. Code will be released.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.09836.title: Can Agentic Systems Close the Gap in Radiology with Production AI Tools?
arXiv|arxiv:2611.09836.abstract: Radiology AI has developed along two paths: specialized models that perform well on narrow tasks but cover few clinical findings, and generalist models that address a broader range of tasks but remain prone to hallucination and inaccurate measurements. Combining the two through agentic systems offers a route towards comprehensive radiology reporting, but published systems are tied to one modality or body part. We describe a radiology agentic framework that standardizes how an orchestrator calls modular tools to produce a structured report, and use it to measure what such a system can do with the tools from FDA-cleared radiology AI devices. Report generation is simulated on a large multi-modality report corpus, with the orchestrator given either a catalog of finding classes consolidated from the cleared devices, each available on the modalities it is cleared for, or an unlimited catalog in which any class can be requested, and planning either from the clinical indication or from the target report. Tool outputs are simulated from the reference report, so the comparison isolates tool availability and orchestration from tool error. With the cleared catalog and the indication alone, the orchestrator recovers under a third of the clinically actionable findings; recovery improves substantially with the unlimited catalog, and further when the plan is written from the target report. Attributing every missed finding to a cause shows that most are classes no cleared device offers for the study's modality, and that a third are classes or tools that were offered and not called. Adding the most frequently missing tools closes most of the gap to the unlimited catalog on held-out reports, whereas a smaller orchestrator with the unlimited catalog gives up the whole gain. Tool availability and effective orchestration are thus complementary constraints on comprehensive AI-assisted radiology reporting.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.07657.title: Where Rules End and Judges Begin: Measuring the Judgment Boundary in Multi-Agent Systems Security
arXiv|arxiv:2610.07657.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) engage tools, share memory, and delegate tasks, often encountering adversarial content. Current defenses for MAS are typically evaluated in isolation, focusing on one attack type at a time, which can lead to costly and hard-to-audit outcomes. This study organizes defenses into five principles, implementing them as DEFER1 (DEterministic-First Enforcement with Residual judgment), which includes a cascade of 28 checks that blocks what it can and refers the rest to a panel of four judges. In independent testing across four domains, attack success rates drop from about 30.0% to approximately 3.0%, with 78% of blocked attacks handled by deterministic checks. Only a quarter of proposals reach the judges in the security-operations domain, illustrating that the rules provide security for attacks violating clear policies, while judges manage those that only misrepresent intent. Both systems have weaknesses, such as a risk-score approval gate that inaccurately approves most attack proposals but few legitimate ones, highlighting the challenges in assessing threats accurately.
